title: Evaluating AI-Assisted Bioinformatics Analyses
text: Free Guide · Updated Oct 2026

title: Preface
text:
Purpose
An AI-assisted analysis may contain convincing explanations and readable code, yet still make claims that its data or methods cannot support. Evaluating it requires scientific judgment and checks that another person can follow.
Evaluating AI-Assisted Bioinformatics Analyses teaches you to inspect an analysis, verify its evidence, and communicate a justified assessment. You will practise recognizing sound reasoning, identifying errors, and explaining uncertainty through original examples drawn from biological data analysis.
This open Complex Data Insights (CDI) guide connects Omics & Bioinformatics with Artificial Intelligence. It supports research practice, independent learning, teaching, and preparation for scientific AI evaluation opportunities.

title: Preface
text:
Who this guide is for
The guide is intended for researchers, postgraduate students, bioinformatics practitioners, educators, and scientific AI evaluation candidates worldwide. No particular institutional affiliation or qualification is required.
You should already be able to:

Read data tables and explain a biological comparison.
Recognize biological replication and interpret basic statistical results.
Read and run a short R script and locate its outputs.

You do not need expertise in every field represented here. For preparation, use the relevant CDI guide: Microbiome, RNA-seq, Single-Cell, Proteomics, or GWAS. The AI Systems guide provides supporting AI concepts.

title: Preface
text:
Scientific scope
Microbiome analysis provides a recurring source of examples, reflecting CDI’s research experience in this field. These examples will explore sample metadata, community profiles, diversity, and the strength of biological claims.
RNA-seq is a second core area, with a guided case addressing experimental design, differential expression, and interpretation. It brings gene-expression analysis into the guide and provides a basis for discussing how evidence is assessed across omics studies. A single-cell case extends the practice to cell-level workflows and annotation.
The shared evaluation framework also applies to proteomics, GWAS, and other bioinformatics settings. Each application requires appropriate domain knowledge and method-specific checks. The worked cases provide depth; they do not define the limits of the guide’s scope.

title: Preface
text:
What you will learn
By completing the exercises, you should be able to:

Identify the scientific question and the evidence needed to answer it.
Check data provenance, study design, methods, and assumptions.
Verify selected outputs and compare them with reported results.
Distinguish supported claims, errors, and unresolved questions.
Write evidence-based feedback with justified corrections.

Every case follows the same process:
Inspect the question → check data and methods → verify results → assess claims → communicate the evaluation.
Reproducing a result does not, by itself, establish that the method or interpretation is appropriate. Your review must address both execution and scientific reasoning.

title: Preface
text:
How to use the guide
Attempt each exercise before consulting its worked explanation. Record the claim reviewed, the check performed, the evidence found, and your proposed action. Explain the consequence of an issue instead of simply marking it wrong.
The core exercises use supplied materials; a paid AI account is not required. Simulated AI responses will be labelled. Form your own initial judgment, then document and verify any optional AI assistance you use.
R verification scripts will live in scripts/R/, with setup instructions provided alongside the completed workflows. Run these scripts separately: rendering the Quarto book displays the lessons without executing the analyses. Distinguish supplied outputs from results you reproduced yourself.






Guide development



The guide is being completed chapter by chapter. Case datasets, scripts, outputs, and worked explanations remain under development until their chapters identify them as available.

title: Preface
text:
Your final deliverable
You will produce an evaluation report documenting your checks, findings, justified corrections, and remaining uncertainty. A reader should be able to tell what you verified and what you could not establish.
The report can support research training or a professional portfolio. Clearly label teaching data, acknowledge assistance, and describe your own contribution.
This open guide stands on its own; separate CDI practicals may provide further assignments. The materials are independent of employer assessments and institutional programmes. Completion develops demonstrable skills without guaranteeing selection, employment, or income.

title: Preface
text:
Before you begin
Identify your strongest biological domain and one skill you need to strengthen. Confirm that you can run a short R script and find its output, then continue to Orientation.

title: Orientation
text:
The reviewer’s role
An AI-assisted bioinformatics analysis can include code, tables, figures, and explanations. Your role is to assess whether these elements agree and whether the evidence supports the scientific conclusion.
These checks apply across microbiome, RNA-seq, single-cell, proteomics, and GWAS analyses, with the methods assessed in their specific context. Review the work at three levels:
A script running successfully answers only part of the first question. A complete review also considers analytical choices and the claims made about their outputs.
Chapter outcome: write a brief evaluation that separates a verified observation, an error, and a claim requiring more evidence.

title: Orientation
text:
Level
Question
Example check




Execution
Does the code perform the stated operation?
Check that a filtering condition matches its description.


Analysis
Is that operation appropriate for the question and data?
Check whether the comparison uses the intended samples.


Interpretation
Does the conclusion follow from the result?
Check whether a descriptive difference is presented as a demonstrated effect.

title: Orientation
text:
Start with the evidence
Before judging a response, identify the scientific question and inventory what you have. An evaluation package may contain:

Data and metadata: measurements, sample identifiers, group labels, and study details.
Code and settings: scripts, parameters, and software information.
Outputs: tables, figures, and execution records.
Response: the explanation or conclusions being evaluated.

Missing material limits what you can establish. If only a results table is available, you can inspect its contents, but you cannot claim to have reproduced the underlying analysis.
When reviewing AI-assisted work, look for problems such as code that disagrees with its explanation, references that cannot be verified, or claims about checks that were never performed. Apply the same evidence standards to human-written and AI-assisted work.

title: Orientation
text:
A first evaluation
The following is an original teaching example. The values are invented and do not represent a biological finding.
Question: What does the supplied table establish about the difference between groups A and B?



Sample
Group
Reported measurement




A1
A
10


A2
A
12


B1
B
14


B2
B
16



No measurement units, study protocol, analysis script, or statistical test are supplied.
Simulated AI response:

The average measurement is 11 in group A and 15 in group B. Group B is therefore 50% higher than group A. This proves that the treatment caused a biologically important increase.


Your task
Evaluate each sentence before opening the worked answer:

Check the two means.
Calculate the percentage increase relative to group A: 100 × (B − A) / A.
Identify what additional evidence is needed to assess the final claim.
Write a corrected conclusion in no more than three sentences.







Worked answer





The means are correct: (10 + 12) / 2 = 11 and (14 + 16) / 2 = 15.
The percentage increase is 100 × (15 − 11) / 11, approximately 36.4%, so the stated 50% is an arithmetic error.
The table alone does not establish a treatment effect or biological importance. We need information about what was measured, how groups were assigned, whether samples are independent, and the uncertainty and biological context of the comparison. We also cannot infer statistical significance from the supplied material.
Corrected conclusion: “In this teaching table, the mean measurement is 11 in group A and 15 in group B, a difference of 4 on the reported measurement scale, or approximately 36.4% relative to group A. These values describe the supplied observations. The available evidence does not establish causation or biological importance.”

title: Orientation
text:
Write feedback that supports action
Useful feedback connects a judgment to evidence and a next step.








Finding
Evidence
Action




Supported calculation
Recalculated means match 11 and 15.
Retain the reported means.


Incorrect calculation
The relative increase is approximately 36.4%.
Correct the percentage and state its reference group.


Unsupported conclusion
Study design and biological context are absent.
Limit the conclusion to description and request the missing evidence.



Notice the distinction between incorrect and not established. The percentage can be corrected directly. The causal claim cannot be resolved from this table alone; that limitation does not prove that no treatment effect exists.

title: Orientation
text:
Checkpoint
Create the results/ folder if needed, then create results/01-orientation-review.md and record your corrected conclusion plus the three findings above in your own words. This is your first review artifact; no analysis script is required for this exercise.
Before continuing, confirm that your review:

Preserves the correct calculation.
Explains the arithmetic error with a checkable correction.
Identifies the unsupported claim without inventing missing evidence.
States what you checked and what remains unresolved.

Continue to Evaluation Framework to apply consistent criteria across larger analyses.

title: Evaluation Framework
text:
Use consistent criteria
A useful evaluation explains both what you concluded and how the evidence supports that judgment. Apply this framework across bioinformatics, adapting each check to the question, data, and method.
Chapter outcome: build an evidence log and prioritize findings using a shared rubric.

title: Evaluation Framework
text:
The evaluation rubric
Begin by stating the question under review in one sentence. Then examine these six areas.








Area
Review question
Evidence to inspect




Question and scope
Does the analysis address the stated question?
Task description, comparison, and intended outcome


Data and provenance
Are the inputs identifiable and suitable?
Data source, sample identifiers, metadata, and exclusions


Design and methods
Do the design and analytical choices support the comparison?
Biological replication, model specification, assumptions, and parameters


Code and results
Do the implemented steps and outputs match the explanation?
Scripts, execution records, tables, and figures


Interpretation
Are claims proportional to the evidence?
Effect estimates, uncertainty, limitations, and biological context


Reporting
Can another reviewer trace and repeat the relevant checks?
File paths, commands, versions, references, and decision records



Record distinct findings separately: a correct calculation and a misreported value need different judgments.

title: Evaluation Framework
text:
Assign a judgment
Label each claim or decision according to the evidence inspected.








Judgment
Meaning
Appropriate response




Supported
The inspected evidence supports the statement within its stated scope.
Retain it and identify the supporting evidence.


Incorrect
A check demonstrates an error or contradiction.
Explain the error and provide a justified correction.


Not established
The evidence is missing or insufficient to decide.
State what is unresolved and request a specific check or source.


Not applicable
The criterion falls outside the defined task.
Explain briefly why it does not apply.



“Supported” does not mean universally true. A description may be supported for a supplied teaching dataset without establishing a general biological conclusion.
Avoid combining these labels into an average score. Several correct details cannot compensate for an error that undermines the main conclusion.

title: Evaluation Framework
text:
Prioritize issues by consequence
Assign a priority to findings that need action. Keep this separate from the judgment label: missing evidence can be as consequential as a demonstrated error.








Priority
Consequence
Suggested action




Blocking
The central result or conclusion cannot currently be relied on.
Resolve before using the conclusion.


Major
A substantial part of the analysis or interpretation needs revision.
Correct or investigate before final reporting.


Minor
Clarity or reporting needs improvement without changing the supported conclusion.
Amend the relevant detail.



These priorities are defined for this guide. Justify them by explaining how each issue affects the analysis or conclusion.

title: Evaluation Framework
text:
Keep an evidence log
Create the results/ folder if needed, then create results/02-evidence-log.tsv with the following column names. You can use a spreadsheet editor or a plain-text editor; separate columns with tabs when saving as TSV.
finding_id  area    claim_or_decision   evidence    check_performed observation judgment    priority    recommended_action
Give evidence a precise location, such as a filename, table row, figure panel, or code section. Describe the check you actually performed. Use none for priority when no corrective action is needed.
A concise entry might read:

F01 — Code and results: The response reports a 50% increase. Recalculation from the supplied means gives approximately 36.4%. Judgment: incorrect. Priority: major because it changes the reported magnitude. Action: correct the percentage and identify group A as the reference.

If you have not run a script, write “inspected code” rather than “reproduced result.” This distinction keeps your review auditable.

title: Evaluation Framework
text:
Practice: matching samples
In this original microbiome teaching example, the intended workflow uses all four samples. The following identifiers are supplied as excerpts; no separate data files are needed for this exercise.

The microbial feature-count table has sample columns S01, S02, S03, and S04.
The metadata contains S01, S02, S03, and S05.
No mapping between S04 and S05 is supplied.
A simulated AI response states: “All four sample identifiers match, so the files are ready for analysis.”

Add two findings to your evidence log:

Evaluate the statement that all identifiers match.
Evaluate whether it would be justified to rename S05 to S04 immediately.

For each, record a judgment, priority, and recommended action before opening the explanation.






Worked explanation





Finding 1: The matching claim is incorrect. Only S01, S02, and S03 occur in both lists. Treat this as blocking for the intended four-sample workflow because the supplied information cannot establish the identity of the remaining sample. Request the sample manifest or another authoritative mapping.
Finding 2: Renaming S05 to S04 is not established as a valid correction. This is also blocking for the intended four-sample workflow. A typographical error is possible, but the identifiers could represent different samples. Resolve their identities before modifying metadata or selecting samples for analysis.
The key distinction is between detecting a mismatch, which the evidence permits, and deciding its cause, which requires more information.

title: Evaluation Framework
text:
Checkpoint
Your completed log should let another reviewer locate the evidence, understand each judgment, and carry out the recommended action. Check that you have:

Separated demonstrated errors from unresolved questions.
Assigned priorities based on scientific consequences.
Proposed corrections without inventing missing information.

Continue to Reproducible Verification to document and run checks systematically.

title: Reproducible Verification
text:
Turn a judgment into a check
A reproducible evaluation records enough detail for another reviewer to repeat a check and compare results. Start with a specific claim, identify the required inputs, and decide what result would support or contradict it.
Chapter outcome: run a sample-matching check, inspect its outputs, and document a finding without changing the original evidence.
This chapter extends the microbiome example from ABE-002. The same identifier checks are useful whenever measurements must be matched to sample metadata, including RNA-seq and other omics workflows.

title: Reproducible Verification
text:
Define the verification boundary
Distinguish three activities in your report:







Activity
What you can claim




Inspect supplied files
You reviewed their contents.


Run a targeted check
You independently checked a specified property or calculation.


Rerun an analysis
You reproduced the stated workflow using the recorded inputs and settings.



None of these alone establishes biological validity. A sample-matching check cannot establish that the samples were collected appropriately or that the chosen statistical model is suitable.

title: Reproducible Verification
text:
Prepare the exercise
Place scripts/R/03-verify-sample-matching.R in your repository. It uses base R and requires no additional packages or downloads. The synthetic identifiers are defined inside the script; no separate dataset is needed.
The feature table identifiers are S01, S02, S03, and S04. The metadata identifiers are S03, S01, S02, and S05. Their order differs, and one identifier differs between the sets.
Simulated AI response:

Both files contain four samples. Their rows can therefore be paired in the current order, and all samples are ready for analysis.

Before running the script, predict which checks will pass. Read the script and identify where it defines inputs, checks identifiers, and writes evidence.

title: Reproducible Verification
text:
Run the verification
Open a terminal in the repository root and run:
Rscript scripts/R/03-verify-sample-matching.R
If Rscript is unavailable in your terminal but R is installed, open an R session, set its working directory to the repository root, and run:
source("scripts/R/03-verify-sample-matching.R")
The script creates results/ch03/ and writes:







Output
Purpose




input-identifiers.tsv
Records the identifiers and order checked.


checks.tsv
Records the result of each check.


sample-membership.tsv
Shows which identifiers occur in each source.


session-info.txt
Records the R environment used.



These files are overwritten on each run. Preserve a copy in a separately named folder before changing inputs. Keep the supplied script unchanged and save any experimental version under a different filename.

title: Reproducible Verification
text:
Interpret the evidence
Open checks.tsv and sample-membership.tsv. A normal script completion means the checks ran; it does not mean that the data passed them.






Expected results and interpretation





The identifiers are present and unique, so the first check passes. The identifier-set and order checks fail.
S04 occurs only in the feature table; S05 occurs only in the metadata. Equal sample counts therefore do not establish matching identities. Reordering alone cannot resolve this mismatch, and renaming an identifier requires an authoritative mapping.
The current-order pairing claim is incorrect. Record the mismatch as blocking for the intended four-sample analysis and request the sample manifest. The check identifies the discrepancy without establishing its cause.



Matching sets and matching order are separate properties. When identifiers are unique and sets match, metadata can be reordered by identifier. This establishes alignment of labels, not proof that the labels describe the correct biological samples.

title: Reproducible Verification
text:
Record your verification
Create results/ch03/verification-note.md with these headings:
# ABE-003 verification note
## Claim reviewed
## Script and command used
## Input identifiers and evidence files
## Observed result
## Judgment, priority, and recommended action
## Limits of this check
Record the script version or Git commit when available. Link your finding to the output filenames and state that the exercise uses synthetic identifiers. If execution fails, record the error and what remains unchecked; do not substitute the expected answer for an observed result.

title: Reproducible Verification
text:
Checkpoint
You are ready to continue when you can explain:

Why equal sample counts do not establish sample matching.
Why matching identifiers and matching order require separate checks.
Which outputs support your finding and which questions remain unresolved.

Retain your note and generated evidence. Continue to the Microbiome Case to apply the framework to a scientific analysis.

title: Microbiome: methods, evidence, and claims
text:
The evaluation question
Do the supplied data support the AI response’s claims about a change in the microbiome?
You will review a synthetic study with four participants, each sampled before and after a dietary change. There is no untreated comparison group, absolute microbial-load measurement, or health outcome. All counts and taxonomic labels are invented teaching materials.
Your task is to verify descriptive results and identify the limits of the conclusions. This is a focused evaluation exercise, not a complete microbiome analysis pipeline.

title: Microbiome: methods, evidence, and claims
text:
Inspect the evidence package
Read cases/microbiome/README.md, then inspect:







File under cases/microbiome/
Role




data/feature-counts.tsv
Read counts for three features across eight samples


data/sample-metadata.tsv
Sample identity, participant identity, and visit


data/taxonomy.tsv
Fictional genus labels


simulated-response.md
Six claims to evaluate


reference/
Independently calculated expected tables


worked-review.md
Worked judgments and corrected interpretation



The verification script is scripts/R/04-verify-microbiome.R. Keep original inputs unchanged. Metadata rows are intentionally arranged differently from count columns, so alignment must use identifiers.
crumbs: 4  Microbiome: methods, evidence, and claims

title: Microbiome: methods, evidence, and claims
text:
Make an initial judgment
Read the simulated response before opening the reference tables or worked review. It claims that the samples are independent, reports changes in F1, and concludes that the dietary change improved health.
Create results/ch04/evidence-log.tsv using the ABE-002 fields. Split statements that combine a valid calculation with an unsupported interpretation into separate findings.
For each claim, ask:

What evidence would establish it?
Can the supplied files answer the question?
What can I check directly, and what remains unresolved?
crumbs: 4  Microbiome: methods, evidence, and claims

title: Microbiome: methods, evidence, and claims
text:
Verify the descriptive results
From the repository root, run:
Rscript scripts/R/04-verify-microbiome.R
Alternatively, from an R session whose working directory is the repository root:
source("scripts/R/04-verify-microbiome.R")
The script needs base R only. It validates identifiers and counts, aligns metadata, checks that each participant has one observation per visit, and calculates per-sample percentages and paired changes. It performs no significance test.
Inspect these files in results/ch04/:

sample-summary.tsv: total reads, F1 reads, and F1 percentage by sample.
paired-changes.tsv: before and after percentages for each participant.
input-checksums.tsv and session-info.txt: input fingerprints and software details.

Outputs are overwritten on rerun. Preserve earlier outputs before experimenting. Compare numeric values and identifiers with the expected tables; harmless formatting differences do not imply different results.






Verification status



The supplied reference tables were independently calculated with Python from the input files. The R script has not been executed in the authoring environment. Record your own execution results; if a check fails, investigate it before accepting the expected answer.
crumbs: 4  Microbiome: methods, evidence, and claims

title: Microbiome: methods, evidence, and claims
text:
Interpret what changed
Read counts and relative abundance answer different questions. A relative abundance is a feature’s share of the measured community; it does not establish its absolute quantity. See Gloor et al. (2017) for the compositional nature of microbiome data.
Check the denominator used in every percentage. Also distinguish the number of samples from the number of participants: two visits from one participant do not create two independent participants.






Worked interpretation





There are eight samples from four participants. Sample identifiers match, but row order differs.
Mean F1 read count rises from 22.5 to 65 while total reads per sample rise from 100 to 200. Mean F1 relative abundance rises from 22.5% to 32.5%: 10 percentage points, or approximately 44.4% relative to the before mean. Every participant has a 10-percentage-point increase.
These are descriptive results for synthetic data. They do not establish an absolute microbial increase, a causal dietary effect, statistical significance, or improved health. Consult cases/microbiome/worked-review.md for judgments on all six claims.
crumbs: 4  Microbiome: methods, evidence, and claims

title: Microbiome: methods, evidence, and claims
text:
Deliverable and checkpoint
Write results/ch04/evaluation-report.md with the question, checks performed, prioritized findings, corrected conclusion, and remaining limitations. Link to your evidence log and output files.
Before continuing, confirm that you preserved supported results, accounted for paired observations, used the correct percentage language, and removed claims requiring evidence that is absent.
Continue to the RNA-seq Case, where you will apply the framework with less guidance.
crumbs: 4  Microbiome: methods, evidence, and claims

title: RNA-seq: design, results, and interpretation
text:
The evaluation question
Can the supplied evidence establish a treatment effect independently of batch?
This case asks you to distinguish a study-design problem from errors in interpreting a results table. Apply the ABE-002 framework with less prompting than in the microbiome case.
Outcome: produce a review that separates estimable comparisons, correct arithmetic, and unsupported biological conclusions.
crumbs: 5  RNA-seq: design, results, and interpretation

title: RNA-seq: design, results, and interpretation
text:
Inspect the case
Read cases/rnaseq/README.md and cases/rnaseq/simulated-response.md. Two evidence components are supplied:








Component
Contents
What it can establish




data/sample-metadata.tsv
Six distinct biological samples: three controls in batch B1 and three treated samples in B2
Replication and overlap between batch and condition


data/illustrative-results.tsv
Six invented gene IDs, log2 fold changes, and p-values
Arithmetic and interpretation checks only



Paths in this table are relative to cases/rnaseq/.
The results table was not generated from these samples or by DESeq2. No count matrix is supplied. Do not infer that the reported numbers validate the intended model, ~ batch + condition.
For the arithmetic exercise, the six rows are the complete testing family. There are no missing p-values or excluded hypotheses. The specified decision rule is Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) adjusted p-value < 0.05.
crumbs: 5  RNA-seq: design, results, and interpretation

title: RNA-seq: design, results, and interpretation
text:
Plan your checks
Create results/ch05/evidence-log.tsv, using the fields from ABE-002. Before running code, identify evidence for each of the seven claims in the simulated response.
Your review should address:

Whether batch and condition can be separated in this design.
Whether changing the formula resolves the scientific limitation.
Which rows satisfy the raw and adjusted p-value rules.
What positive and negative log2 fold changes mean.
Whether any supplied number supports a biological treatment claim.

Preserve supported statements and separate mixed claims into individual findings.
crumbs: 5  RNA-seq: design, results, and interpretation

title: RNA-seq: design, results, and interpretation
text:
Run targeted verification
From the repository root:
Rscript scripts/R/05-verify-rnaseq.R
Alternatively, from an R session with the repository root as its working directory:
source("scripts/R/05-verify-rnaseq.R")
The script requires base R only. It constructs the design matrix, checks its rank, calculates BH-adjusted values with p.adjust(), and converts log2 fold changes with 2^log2FoldChange. It does not fit a differential-expression model.







Output under results/ch05/
Use




batch-condition-table.tsv
Inspect overlap between conditions and batches.


design-matrix.tsv, design-check.tsv
Inspect the model columns and rank.


result-checks.tsv
Inspect adjusted values, threshold decisions, and fold changes.


input-checksums.tsv, session-info.txt
Record input fingerprints and software details.



Outputs are overwritten on rerun. Preserve earlier runs before changing inputs. A completed script can report a failed design check: completion is not approval of the analysis.






Verification status



The reference tables in cases/rnaseq/reference/ were calculated independently with Python. The R script has not been executed in the authoring environment. Compare your observed results with the references; do not report expected values as an execution you performed.
crumbs: 5  RNA-seq: design, results, and interpretation

title: RNA-seq: design, results, and interpretation
section: Interpret the design before the claims
text:
Interpret the design before the claims
A full-rank design matrix is required to estimate its coefficients separately. Here, the treated-condition indicator and batch-B2 indicator are identical. Adding both terms cannot distinguish their effects. Dropping batch does not make the condition comparison unconfounded. The DESeq2 documentation explains this under “Model matrix not full rank.”
For the separate arithmetic task, check all six p-values together. A correct multiple-testing calculation cannot repair an unsuitable design or establish the provenance of invented results.






Verification checkpoints





The design has six rows, three columns, and rank two. Separate batch and condition effects are not estimable.
Four raw p-values are below 0.05. The BH-adjusted values are 0.006, 0.03, 0.06, 0.06, 0.24, and 0.8; only G1 and G2 meet the adjusted threshold.
A log2 fold change of 1 corresponds to a ratio of 2. A value of -1 corresponds to 0.5, not negative expression.
These statements establish design properties and arithmetic only. Compare your complete review with cases/rnaseq/worked-review.md after finishing your first attempt.
crumbs: 5  RNA-seq: design, results, and interpretation

title: RNA-seq: design, results, and interpretation
text:
Deliverable and checkpoint
Write results/ch05/evaluation-report.md, linking your evidence log and outputs. Include a corrected conclusion and a precise request for the evidence or design changes needed before making treatment-specific claims.
Your report should distinguish a calculation error, a design limitation, and a missing-evidence problem. Explain why a small adjusted p-value cannot resolve the latter two.
Continue to the Single-Cell Case for more independent evaluation.
crumbs: 5  RNA-seq: design, results, and interpretation

title: Single-cell: replication, annotation, and uncertainty
text:
Your evaluation brief
Does the supplied single-cell evidence support the response’s claims about treatment, cell identity, and analysis quality?
This original synthetic case contains 2,000 retained cells from four donors, with two donors per condition. Cell assignments and marker summaries are invented. No clinical outcome, randomization, raw expression matrix, or full analysis workflow is supplied.
Your task is to decide which statements are supported, incorrect, or not established. Choose and justify your own checks before consulting the worked review.
crumbs: 6  Single-cell: replication, annotation, and uncertainty

title: Single-cell: replication, annotation, and uncertainty
text:
Inventory the evidence
Start with cases/singlecell/README.md and cases/singlecell/simulated-response.md.







File in cases/singlecell/data/
Contents




donors.tsv
Donor identity and condition


cells.tsv
Cell identity, donor identity, and assigned cluster


marker-evidence.tsv
Supplied detection percentages for three fictional markers in C1


teaching-marker-reference.tsv
Expected marker combinations for two fictional candidate types



The marker summaries are separate supplied evidence: they cannot be recalculated from a table containing only cell labels. The marker names and candidate types are teaching devices, not real biological annotations.
crumbs: 6  Single-cell: replication, annotation, and uncertainty

title: Single-cell: replication, annotation, and uncertainty
text:
Plan an independent review
Create results/ch06/evidence-log.tsv using the ABE-002 fields. For each of the seven claims, specify the relevant evidence, your intended check, and the consequence if the claim is wrong.
Consider the biological unit of replication, how unequal cell contributions affect summaries, whether annotation evidence distinguishes candidates, and which workflow claims require missing records.
Write an initial conclusion before running code. Do not assume that every statement in the simulated response is wrong.
crumbs: 6  Single-cell: replication, annotation, and uncertainty

title: Single-cell: replication, annotation, and uncertainty
text:
Verify selected properties
Run from the repository root:
Rscript scripts/R/06-verify-singlecell.R
Or use an R session with the repository root as its working directory:
source("scripts/R/06-verify-singlecell.R")
The script requires base R only. It validates cell-to-donor mappings, summarizes C1 proportions by donor and condition, and compares marker patterns under the exercise’s fictional reference. It performs no clustering, differential-expression test, or biological annotation validation.
Inspect these outputs under results/ch06/:







Output
Review purpose




donor-summary.tsv
Compare the number of cells and C1 proportion contributed by each donor.


condition-summary.tsv
Contrast pooled proportions with unweighted donor means.


teaching-marker-check.tsv
Compare observed high-detection markers with each candidate pattern.


input-checksums.tsv, session-info.txt
Record input fingerprints and software details.



Outputs are overwritten on rerun. Preserve prior results before changing inputs. In this exercise, “high detection” means at least 50%; this is a teaching convention, not a recommended universal annotation threshold.






Verification status



Reference tables were calculated independently with Python. The R script has not been executed in the authoring environment. Record your actual results and investigate discrepancies before accepting the expected values.
crumbs: 6  Single-cell: replication, annotation, and uncertainty

title: Single-cell: replication, annotation, and uncertainty
text:
Distinguish the questions being answered
A pooled proportion describes all retained cells combined. An unweighted donor mean gives each donor equal weight. Neither summary alone establishes a population-level treatment effect.
For comparisons across donors, cells from one donor must not be treated as independent donor replicates. Squair et al. (2021) demonstrate why accounting for biological replication matters in single-cell differential-expression analysis. This case checks replication and descriptive proportions; it does not implement a differential-expression method.
Similarly, a marker shared by two candidates does not distinguish them. Evaluate the full supplied pattern and state the limits of a provisional label. Missing QC records leave quality claims unverified; they do not prove that QC failed.
crumbs: 6  Single-cell: replication, annotation, and uncertainty

title: Single-cell: replication, annotation, and uncertainty
text:
Submit your evaluation
Write results/ch06/evaluation-report.md with:

The question and scope of your review.
Checks performed, evidence locations, and prioritized findings.
A corrected interpretation of proportions and annotation evidence.
Specific requests for missing information and remaining uncertainty.

Explain whether the pooled and donor-level summaries answer the same question. Identify at least one statement worth retaining.






Self-check after completing your report





C1 proportions by donor are 20%, 80%, 80%, and 20%. Each condition has an unweighted donor mean of 50%, but pooled proportions are 74% for controls and 26% for treated cells because donors contribute unequal numbers of cells. Equal means here do not demonstrate biological equivalence.
M1 is shared by both fictional candidates. The combined pattern favors a provisional Type_B-like label within the exercise. It does not establish a real cell identity.
Compare all seven judgments with cases/singlecell/worked-review.md. Revise your report where evidence warrants it and explain your changes.



Continue to Independent Evaluation to bring the framework and reporting skills together.

title: Independent Evaluation
text:
Your assignment
Complete a review of an unfamiliar simulated AI response using the framework developed in this guide. You will choose the checks, prioritize the findings, and write a corrected scientific conclusion.
The supplied assignment uses a new synthetic microbiome example. Its purpose is to test transferable evaluation skills: checking denominators, identifying replication, separating measurements from claims, and documenting uncertainty.
Outcome: a concise evaluation report supported by an evidence log and repeatable checks.

title: Independent Evaluation
text:
Start with the brief
Read cases/independent/brief.md. It contains the scenario, complete six-sample table, six response statements, and submission requirements. No external dataset or paid AI account is needed.
Do not open cases/independent/self-review.md until you have saved your initial report. A calculator, spreadsheet, or short script is sufficient. Choose the tool you can use reliably and retain enough detail for another person to repeat your calculations.
This is an independent practice task, not a formal assessment of eligibility for employment or specialist projects.

title: Independent Evaluation
text:
Prepare your review files
Create results/ch07/ and copy these templates into it:







Supplied template
Save your working copy as




templates/independent-evaluation-report.qmd
results/ch07/evaluation-report.qmd


templates/independent-evidence-log.tsv
results/ch07/evidence-log.tsv


templates/independent-self-assessment.md
results/ch07/self-assessment.md



The templates are deliberately brief. Replace prompts with your own findings, and keep the supplied originals available for reuse. The report can remain a QMD source file; a separate rendered report is optional and is not part of the book’s chapter list.

title: Independent Evaluation
text:
Carry out the evaluation
Work through the task without relying on a prewritten verification script:

Define the scope. State the question and identify what the supplied evidence can address.
Extract claims. Separate observations, calculations, analytical decisions, and biological conclusions.
Verify. Complete at least two quantitative checks and record formulas, commands, or calculation notes.
Judge. Apply the ABE-002 labels and justify priorities by scientific consequence.
Communicate. Retain supported statements, explain corrections, and specify the evidence needed for unresolved claims.

Write your initial judgment before using optional AI assistance. If you use assistance later, record its role and verify any suggestions adopted. Do not represent assisted work as an unaided assessment.

title: Independent Evaluation
text:
Keep the report focused
Aim for approximately 500–800 words, excluding the evidence table and calculation records. Include the scope, main findings, corrected conclusion, and limitations. A longer report is useful only when it adds necessary evidence or explanation.
Every consequential finding should identify a claim, point to evidence, explain its scientific impact, and recommend a specific action. Avoid repeating the same limitation in several sections.
Your corrected conclusion should be understandable without opening the full evidence log. Your supporting files should allow a reviewer to verify how you reached it.

title: Independent Evaluation
text:
Review and revise
Save an initial copy, such as evaluation-report-initial.qmd, before opening the self-review. Compare your reasoning and calculations, then complete the self-assessment rubric.
Use Ready when the criterion is supported by your work and Revise when it needs attention. These labels are formative; they do not certify competence. Resolve numerical errors and issues that could change the central conclusion before finalizing the report.
If your judgment differs from the worked review, return to the evidence and explain the difference. Reasonable wording or priority choices can vary; unsupported conclusions still require correction.

title: Independent Evaluation
text:
Final checkpoint
Your completed submission should contain:

An initial report and a revised final report.
An evidence log covering all six response statements.
Calculation records or scripts for your quantitative checks.
A self-assessment and a short explanation of revisions.

Label the work as a synthetic CDI teaching exercise if you share it in a portfolio. Describe your own contribution and retain relevant attribution.
Continue to Next Steps to plan further practice and present your evaluation work professionally.

title: Next Steps
text:
Take stock of your evidence
You have practised inspecting claims, performing targeted checks, and communicating scientific judgments. The next step is to identify which skills your completed work demonstrates and which need further practice.
Review your ABE-007 report and self-assessment. Select one finding you handled well and one you revised substantially. Explain what made the first defensible and what changed your reasoning in the second.
Chapter outcome: prepare a clear description of your evaluation work and a focused development plan.

title: Next Steps
text:
Choose your next learning need
Use difficulties encountered during the exercises to choose your next task.








If you struggled with…
Practise next
Evidence of progress




Identifying samples and replication
Reconstruct a sample-to-participant map and check repeated observations.
A verified metadata summary and explanation of the experimental unit.


Study design and statistical interpretation
Review a comparison, its assumptions, and the conclusions it permits.
A justified design critique with appropriate limitations.


Running verification code
Repeat a small check from a clean session and document inputs and commands.
Reproducible outputs and an execution record.


Biological interpretation
Compare a claim with its supporting results and domain references.
A corrected claim that states uncertainty.


Communicating findings
Rewrite a long review around its most consequential issues.
A concise report with traceable evidence and specific actions.



Choose one priority at a time. Completing another exercise is most useful when you can explain what improved.

title: Next Steps
text:
Extend the scientific scope
Microbiome and RNA-seq provide substantial opportunities for deeper practice. You can also apply the framework to single-cell analysis, proteomics, GWAS, or another field in which you have suitable preparation.
Use the relevant CDI guide to strengthen the underlying analysis skills:

Microbiome Analysis System
RNA-Seq Analysis System
Single-Cell Analysis System
Proteomics Analysis System
GWAS Analysis System

Start with one bounded question, such as whether metadata support a comparison or whether a reported result matches its code. Expand your review as your domain knowledge grows. The framework provides consistent questions; each method still requires its own scientific checks.
For practice beyond this guide, use original teaching materials or openly available data and code with suitable permissions. Record provenance and distinguish the original analysis from any errors you introduce for an exercise.

title: Next Steps
text:
Present a portfolio example
Select one completed evaluation and package it so another person can understand the question, inspect your checks, and assess your judgment.







Portfolio component
What to include




Short overview
The question, teaching context, and your contribution.


Evaluation report
Supported findings, corrections, priorities, and limitations.


Evidence
Inputs or permitted source links, verification code or calculations, and outputs.


Reproduction notes
Commands, software details, and input versions where available.


Reflection
Changes made after review and remaining learning needs.



Label synthetic data and simulated AI responses clearly. Distinguish a targeted verification exercise from a complete analytical pipeline. State whether you inspected supplied results, independently recalculated them, or reran a workflow.
A credible description might be:

Evaluated a synthetic AI-assisted microbiome analysis by checking sample structure, recalculating relative abundances, and reviewing the biological claims. Produced an evidence log and corrected interpretation, with documented limitations and disclosure of assistance.

Adapt this description to work you actually completed. Preserve CDI attribution and disclose any assistance used. Check permissions before sharing externally sourced data or code.

title: Next Steps
section: Apply the skills in different settings
text:
Apply the skills in different settings
The same evidence-based review process can support research discussions, teaching, peer feedback, and scientific AI evaluation tasks. Tailor your report to the reader’s question while keeping its evidence and limitations explicit.
For an external assessment or project, follow its specific rules on independent work, AI assistance, confidentiality, and reporting. This guide is an independent learning resource; completion does not establish employer approval, certification, project access, or income.

title: Next Steps
text:
Make a short development plan
Create results/08-development-plan.md and answer:

Which evaluation skill can I now demonstrate, and where is the evidence?
Which limitation in my work matters most?
What specific practice task will address it?
What output will show improvement, and when will I review it?

Keep the plan to one page. Return to your evidence after the next task and revise the plan based on what you can demonstrate.
Use the Appendix for supporting reference material and the References for the guide’s bibliography.

title: Appendix
text:
Understand the outputs
A script completing successfully means its instructions ran. Some exercises deliberately report failed checks, such as mismatched identifiers or a rank-deficient design. Read the findings before deciding whether an analysis is usable.
The scripts overwrite their named outputs on rerun. Preserve previous results before changing inputs. Keep original teaching files separate from experimental copies, and document any modification.
Reference tables for ABE-004 through ABE-006 were calculated independently with Python. The R scripts were not executed in the authoring environment. Record your own observed results and software details; expected tables are comparison aids, not proof of an R execution.

title: Appendix
text:
Evaluation labels







Label
Use when…




Supported
Inspected evidence supports the claim within its stated scope.


Incorrect
A check demonstrates an error or contradiction.


Not established
Evidence is insufficient to decide.


Not applicable
A criterion falls outside the task; give a reason.



For issues requiring action, assign Blocking, Major, or Minor according to scientific consequence. Use none when no correction is needed. Split statements that combine correct calculations with unsupported conclusions.

title: Appendix
text:
Troubleshooting







Problem
First check or action




Rscript is not found
Check whether R is installed and accessible from the terminal. Alternatively, use source("scripts/R/<script-name>.R") in an R session opened at the repository root, replacing the placeholder with the actual filename.


An input file cannot be opened
Check your working directory and the extracted folder structure. In R, getwd() shows the current directory.


An assertion fails
Inspect the message and corresponding input. Do not remove the check merely to let the script continue.


Results differ from a reference
Compare input versions, identifiers, denominators, and numeric precision. Save the discrepancy before editing anything.


A chapter link cannot be resolved
Confirm that both the link and _quarto.yml use the current filename. Microbiome is 04-microbiome-case.qmd; RNA-seq is 05-rnaseq-case.qmd.


Rendering produces no analysis outputs
Run the verification scripts separately. Display-only code fences and eval: false keep analysis execution separate from book rendering.



A genuine error may be in the input, environment, or supplied script. Document it before proposing a correction.

templates/independent-evaluation-report.qmd

title: Appendix
text:
Sharing checklist
Before sharing an evaluation, confirm that another reader can locate its evidence and distinguish:

Synthetic teaching materials from research data.
Supplied outputs from independently reproduced results.
Confirmed errors from missing evidence.
Your own work from assistance received.

Include input versions or fingerprints, software details where relevant, and unresolved limitations. Consult References for sources supporting the case-study concepts.

title: Appendix
text:
Scientific foundations

Microbiome interpretation: Relative abundance describes composition and does not directly establish absolute microbial quantities (Gloor et al. 2017).
RNA-seq study design: Complete confounding prevents separate estimation of batch and condition effects (Analyzing RNA-seq Data with DESeq2 n.d.).
Single-cell replication: Comparisons across conditions must account for biological replication rather than treating cells from the same donor as independent biological replicates (Squair et al. 2021).
